subject: Computing
board: National Curriculum (aligned to Edexcel GCSE Computer Science 1CP2)
source: Drive 'Computing Overview' Year 7 scheme (Intro to Scratch: Introduction, Variables and IF statements, Variables and operators, The Scratch Calculator), National Curriculum KS3, aligned to Edexcel GCSE Computer Science 1CP2 | Spring 1 2027 (lessons 5 to 9, v3): Tarbiyyah Secondary Computing and ICT Curriculum Intent, Year 7 (Think like a computer: algorithms); diagrams.net; building to Pearson Edexcel 4CP0

lessons.title: Introduction to Scratch: sprites, movement and input
objectives: Create and control sprites and backdrops in Scratch
Explain the terms sequence, event and input

keywords.def: an object or character that a Scratch program controls
instructions carried out one after another in order
something that triggers a script, such as a key press
data given to a program by the user or a device

starter: Give one example of an input device and one output device.
Why does the order of instructions matter in a program?

teach.heading: The Scratch environment
teach.note: Share your screen with Scratch open. Show how to add a sprite, change the backdrop and drag blocks. Pupils should have a free Scratch account or use the offline editor. Remind them to save regularly.

teach.heading: Events and sequence
bullets: 'When green flag clicked' starts a script.
teach.note: Build: when flag clicked, go to x:0 y:0, say Hello for 2 seconds, move 50 steps. Swap two blocks and run it again to show that order matters. Ask pupils to predict the result before each run.

teach.heading: Keyboard input
bullets: 'When right arrow key pressed' is an event.
teach.note: Demonstrate four scripts for the arrow keys using change x and change y. Introduce the coordinates: the stage centre is (0,0), x goes left to right, y goes bottom to top. Misconception: pupils confuse x and y; ask them to point along each axis.

teach.heading: Debug a script
bullets: Fix one problem at a time.
teach.note: Show a script where up and down are swapped. Ask pupils to find the bug. Reinforce the habit of testing and tracing. Mention that patience and carefulness are part of good character (sabr and ihsan) when we debug.

practice: On the stage, what are the coordinates of the centre? What does change x by 10 do?
Predict: when flag clicked, move 100 steps, turn 90 degrees, move 100 steps. Draw the path.
Which block would you use to make a sprite say 'Assalamu alaykum' for 3 seconds?
independent: Build a script so a sprite moves in four directions using the arrow keys.
Add a backdrop and a second sprite that says 'Welcome!' when the space key is pressed.
Stretch: add a sound that plays each time the sprite moves, and make the sprite stay within the stage edges.
exit: Name one event block and say what it does.
What is the difference between a sprite and a backdrop?
lessons.homework: Create a Scratch project where a sprite navigates a simple maze with the arrow keys. Share a screenshot.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a labelled screenshot of the Scratch interface and a word bank; give partially built scripts. Stretch: add a rule that sends the sprite back to the start when it touches a wall colour.

lessons.title: Variables and IF statements
objectives: Store user input in a variable
Use IF and IF-ELSE statements with a condition
Build a guessing game that uses selection

keywords.def: a named store for data that can change while a program runs
choosing which instructions to run based on a condition
a statement that is either true or false
chosen by chance, with no pattern

starter: Bismillah. What is the output of: set score to 3, change score by 4?
Which keyboard events did we use last lesson?
Is 'x > 5' a true/false condition? When is it true?

teach.heading: Variables store data
bullets: set secret to a random number.
The value can change as the program runs.
teach.note: Create the variable and show it on the stage. Use pick random 1 to 10. Run several times to show different values. Link to Year 5 learning: variable = labelled box.

teach.heading: Ask and answer
bullets: Store it: set guess to answer.
teach.note: Show that answer changes each time something is asked, so we store it in a variable called guess if we need it later. This is a misconception many pupils have: answer is overwritten by the next ask.

teach.heading: IF and IF-ELSE
bullets: The condition is true or false.
teach.note: Build the guessing game. Run it with a right and wrong guess. Show also guess > secret to give hints (too high). Introduce comparison operators: <, >, =.

teach.heading: Test thoroughly
bullets: Test a guess that is too high.
Test a guess that is too low.
teach.note: Create a test table on screen: input, expected output, actual output. This is a skill needed at GCSE. Ask pupils to find a test case which might break the game (e.g. typing text).

practice: Is the condition true? x = 7: x > 5, x = 5, x < 7.
What is wrong with this: IF answer = secret, but secret was never set? (the program compares with an empty or old value)
Write the IF-ELSE for a game which says 'Pass' when score >= 50 else 'Fail'.
independent: Build a number guessing game with a random number from 1 to 10.
Add hints: 'too high' or 'too low' using nested IF blocks.
Stretch: add a variable to count the number of guesses and show it at the end.
exit: Write one test for your guessing game with the input and the expected output.
lessons.homework: Make the guessing game harder by using a bigger range of numbers (1 to 50). Test it and write down three test cases.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a flow diagram of the program with sentences to complete. Stretch: let the game tell the player how close they are (within 3 or not).

lessons.title: Variables and operators
objectives: Use more than one variable in a program
Combine conditions using AND, OR and NOT

keywords.def: a symbol or block that performs a calculation or comparison
true only if both conditions are true
true if at least one condition is true
reverses true to false and false to true

starter: Bismillah. What is the value of x after: set x to 2, change x by 3?
What is a condition? Give one example.

teach.heading: Arithmetic operators
teach.note: Build a small script which asks two numbers and says the total. Test with 3 and 4 (7). Point out the difference between the + operator (3 and 4 make 7) and the 'join' block (3 and 4 make 34). Misconception: pupils use join when they mean add.

teach.heading: Two variables
teach.note: Rebuild the script using a, b and total. Explain why storing values in variables is better than using answer directly. Pupils should trace the program with a trace table for inputs 6 and 9.

teach.heading: Combining conditions
teach.note: Use a truth table with two inputs. Ask pupils when 'A AND B' is true (only when both are). Link to logic gates covered later at GCSE. Misconception: pupils think OR means exactly one is true; it also includes both.

teach.heading: Mod: remainders
bullets: If n mod 2 = 0 then n is even.
teach.note: Demonstrate an even-or-odd checker. Explain mod gives the remainder after division. This idea returns in GCSE programming as the modulus operator.

independent: Build a program that asks for two numbers and tells the user their sum, difference and product.
Build an even/odd checker using mod and an IF-ELSE.
Stretch: make a program which tells you if a number is between 10 and 20 using AND.
lessons.homework: Design a program on paper which asks the user for their age and uses AND to decide whether they are in the 11 to 14 age band.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a truth table template and colour-coded blocks for AND/OR. Stretch: use mod to make a program that checks whether a number is divisible by 3.

lessons.title: The Scratch calculator and flowcharts
objectives: Draw a flowchart using standard symbols
Build a calculator that chooses an operation
Test and evaluate a program against its design

keywords.def: a diagram that shows the steps of an algorithm using symbols
the start or end symbol (rounded box) in a flowchart
a diamond symbol with a yes/no question
a rectangle showing an action or calculation

starter: Name the three types of programming structure (sequence, selection, ___).

teach.heading: Flowchart symbols
teach.note: Draw each symbol on screen and give an example. These symbols are used in GCSE Computer Science exams. Ask pupils to say which symbol would show 'ask for number 1'. Parallelogram.

teach.heading: Flowchart for a calculator
teach.note: Build the flowchart step by step. Show how decisions chain: if not +, check -, then *, then /. Ask pupils to trace through with 8, 2 and '*' (16).

teach.heading: Build the calculator
bullets: Ask for two numbers and an operator.
teach.note: Convert the flowchart to Scratch blocks. Point out how each diamond becomes an IF block. Take care with division by zero: ask what should happen if number 2 is 0 and let pupils suggest adding a check.

teach.heading: Test and improve
bullets: Compare the result with the flowchart.
teach.note: Use the test table again: input, expected, actual. Ask: does the program do what the design says? Invite pupils to describe one improvement. Linking to honesty in work: we check our work thoroughly rather than just hoping it is right.

practice: Which flowchart symbol is used for 'Is the number even?'
Trace the calculator with 12, 4 and '/'. What is the output? (3)
Why must we check for division by zero?
independent: Draw a flowchart for a calculator that adds or subtracts two numbers.
Build the calculator in Scratch with four operators and test it with at least 6 test cases.
Stretch: add a check for division by zero that displays a friendly error message.
exit: Give one test case for the calculator and its expected output.
lessons.homework: Draw a flowchart for a program that decides whether a number typed by the user is positive, negative or zero.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a flowchart with missing text to complete and a symbol key. Stretch: draw the flowchart for a program that works out the area of either a rectangle or a triangle.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Think like a computer: algorithms
lessons.title: What is an algorithm?
lessons.bigQuestion: Is a recipe an algorithm? What would make a recipe fail for someone who has never cooked?
objectives: To understand what an algorithm is and why it must be precise, ordered and unambiguous
successCriteria: All: define an algorithm and give an everyday example
Most: write an unambiguous algorithm for a simple task
Some: explain how an ambiguous instruction leads to a different result
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: the written method for long multiplication is an algorithm
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the ordered steps of wudu and salah, done precisely and in sequence

keywords.def: a precise sequence of steps to solve a problem
having only one possible meaning
a single step that tells someone what to do
data given to an algorithm
the result an algorithm produces

hook.text: Is a recipe an algorithm? What would make a recipe fail for someone who has never cooked?
hook.a: Yes: it is ordered steps. Vague steps ('cook until done') fail a beginner; precise ones do not.

starter.q: What does CPU stand for?
Name one input device and one output device.
What is the job of the CPU?
starter.a: To process instructions (fetch, decode and execute them).

starter.q: What is binary?
starter.a: A number system using only 0 and 1.

teach.heading: Algorithms everywhere
bullets: A sequence of steps to solve a problem
teach.note: A computer cannot guess what you meant: it follows every step literally. An algorithm is the plan; a program is the algorithm written in code.

teach.heading: Precise and unambiguous
bullets: Steps are in the right order
teach.note: Unplugged: the teacher follows pupils' 'make a jam sandwich' steps literally on camera (with real bread) and gets it wrong on purpose.

misconception.wrong: 'Put jam on the bread' is a clear instruction
misconception.right: It is ambiguous: open the jar? which side? how much? spread with what? Precise steps say each one

teach.heading: Input, process, output
teach.note: Example: making tea.

teach.heading: Model: an unambiguous algorithm
bullets: Test it by following it literally
teach.note: Write it with the class.

model.problem: Algorithm: find the largest of three numbers 4, 9, 6.
steps: Set largest to the first number (4)
Compare with the next (9): bigger, so largest = 9
Compare with the next (6): not bigger, keep 9

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.why: Only '2 teaspoons' has one meaning; 'some', 'a while' and 'properly' can be read many ways.

practice.q: Rewrite 'walk to the door' as precise steps for a robot in your room.
practice.a: For example: stand, turn left 90 degrees, walk 4 steps forward, stop.
practice.model: Teacher writes: '1. Stand up. 2. Turn right 90 degrees. 3. Walk forward 3 steps. 4. Stop.' and explains each is one action with numbers.

practice.q: Find the ambiguity: 'Take the second left after the big tree.'
practice.a: Which tree counts as big? Is a footpath a 'left'?

practice.q: Give the input and output of 'count the vowels in a word'.
practice.a: Input: a word; output: the number of vowels.

independent.q: Core: Write an unambiguous algorithm (6 to 10 numbered steps) to make a cup of tea in the portal response box.
independent.a: Numbered single actions with quantities and order: fill kettle, boil, teabag in cup, pour, wait 3 minutes, remove bag, add milk.
independent.model: Teacher writes steps 1 and 2: '1. Fill the kettle with 300 ml of water. 2. Switch the kettle on and wait until it switches off.'

independent.q: Extend: Write an algorithm to find the smallest of five numbers. Test it on 7, 3, 9, 1, 5.
independent.a: Set smallest to first; compare each next number; replace if smaller; output smallest = 1.

independent.q: Stretch: Explain why a computer needs more precise instructions than a person.
independent.a: A person uses common sense to fill gaps; a computer only does exactly what it is told.

exit.q: An algorithm is... A) a computer B) a precise sequence of steps C) a programming language
exit.a: B) a precise sequence of steps

exit.q: Big question: is a recipe an algorithm? Give one reason a recipe might fail.
exit.a: Yes; it fails if a step is ambiguous, such as 'cook until done'.

lessons.homework: Write the algorithm for getting from your front door to the nearest shop or masjid in at most 10 precise steps.
lessons.send: SEND: step frame with numbered boxes. EAL: precise, ambiguous, sequence with examples. Stretch: write the 'smallest number' algorithm so it works for any list length.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Think like a computer: algorithms
lessons.title: Decomposition and abstraction
lessons.bigQuestion: The London Underground map is not accurate: distances and bends are wrong. Why is it still so useful?
objectives: To understand how decomposition and abstraction make a large problem easier to solve
successCriteria: All: break a problem into smaller parts
Most: remove unnecessary detail from a problem (abstraction)
Some: apply both to plan a solution to a real problem
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: the London Underground map is an abstraction of real geography
lessons.smsc: Social: planning a family task (a dinner for guests) together by sharing the parts

keywords.def: breaking a problem into smaller parts
removing detail that does not matter
ways of thinking to solve problems like a computer scientist
one smaller part of a big problem

hook.text: The London Underground map is not accurate: distances and bends are wrong. Why is it still so useful?
hook.a: It keeps only what travellers need (lines, stations, order): that is abstraction.

starter.q: What is an algorithm?
starter.a: A precise sequence of steps to solve a problem.

starter.q: What does unambiguous mean?
Give the input and output of a sat nav.
starter.a: Input: start and destination; output: directions.

starter.q: Make precise: 'add a bit of salt'.
starter.a: For example: add 1/4 teaspoon of salt.

teach.heading: Decomposition
bullets: Break a big problem into parts
teach.note: Example: planning a school open day online: invitations, timetable, slides, tech check.

teach.heading: Abstraction
teach.note: The Tube map: keeps lines, stations and order; drops real distances and streets.

teach.heading: Which details matter?
bullets: Colour of the train does not
teach.note: Sort as a class.

teach.heading: Model: both together
teach.note: Talk it through.

steps: Decompose: ask a question, get the answer, check it, keep score, show score
Abstract: a question is just two numbers and their product
Ignore: colours, sounds, the user's name
Each part becomes a small algorithm
model.answer: Five sub-problems, each modelled with only the numbers that matter

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: Removing unnecessary detail from a problem is called...
check.why: Decomposition breaks a problem up; abstraction removes detail that does not matter.

practice.q: Decompose 'getting ready for school online' into at least four parts.
practice.a: For example: wake for Fajr, breakfast, set up the device and log in to Teams, prepare books and pens.
practice.model: Teacher decomposes 'make breakfast' into: choose food, prepare it, eat, tidy, and shows each part could be split again.

practice.q: A map for a fire drill: which details would you keep?
practice.a: Exits, routes, the meeting point; not furniture colours.

practice.q: Is the Tube map decomposition or abstraction?

independent.q: Core: Decompose 'plan a family trip to the park' into at least five sub-problems in the portal response box.
independent.a: For example: date and weather, transport, food, prayer times and place, what to bring.
independent.model: Teacher writes the first two sub-problems and why each is separate.

independent.q: Extend: For one sub-problem, list the details to keep and to remove (abstraction).
independent.a: Transport: keep start, destination, bus number, times; remove bus colour, driver's name.

independent.q: Stretch: Explain why programmers decompose before they code.
independent.a: Small parts are easier to solve, test and share between people; mistakes are easier to find.

exit.q: Breaking a problem into smaller parts is... A) abstraction B) decomposition C) output
Big question: why is the Tube map useful even though it is not accurate?
exit.a: It is an abstraction: it keeps only lines, stations and order, which is all a traveller needs.

lessons.homework: Decompose one household job (for example preparing for Jumu'ah) into sub-problems and underline the details that matter.
lessons.send: SEND: partly filled decomposition diagram. EAL: decompose, abstract, detail with pictures. Stretch: decompose a game into sub-problems.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Think like a computer: algorithms
lessons.title: Sequence, selection and iteration
lessons.bigQuestion: Every program ever written is built from just three ideas. What do you think they are?
objectives: To understand how sequence, selection and iteration are the building blocks of every algorithm
successCriteria: All: identify sequence, selection and iteration in an algorithm
Most: write an algorithm that uses all three
Some: trace an algorithm with a loop and a condition to find its output
lessons.crossCurricular: Islamic Studies: the rak'ahs of salah follow a sequence and repeat, with set choices (for example the number of rak'ahs)
lessons.smsc: Moral: making good decisions (selection) in daily life

keywords.def: steps carried out in order
a decision: IF a condition is true, do one thing, ELSE another
repeating steps, also called a loop
a statement that is true or false

hook.text: Every program ever written is built from just three ideas. What do you think they are?
hook.a: Doing steps in order, making decisions and repeating: sequence, selection, iteration.

starter.q: Removing unnecessary detail is called...
What is decomposition?
starter.a: Breaking a problem into smaller parts.

starter.q: Give one feature of a good algorithm.
What is the output of 'find the largest of 3, 8, 5'?

teach.heading: Sequence
bullets: Change the order, change the result
teach.note: Wudu has a set order; doing it out of order is a different algorithm.

teach.heading: Selection
teach.note: Condition: a true or false question.

code.text:
INPUT temperature
IF temperature < 10 THEN
    OUTPUT "Wear a coat"
ELSE
    OUTPUT "No coat needed"
ENDIF

teach.heading: Iteration
teach.note: Two kinds of loop.

code.text:
total = 0
FOR i = 1 TO 5
    total = total + i
NEXT i
OUTPUT total

teach.heading: Model: trace it
teach.note: Trace table with the class.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: 'Keep stirring until the sugar dissolves' is an example of...
check.why: It repeats until a condition is met: a loop. It has a condition, but the action repeats, so it is iteration.

practice.q: Label each line: 'Fill kettle. IF kettle is full THEN switch on. Repeat: check if boiled.'
practice.model: Teacher labels line by line: one action in order = sequence; IF = selection; repeat = iteration.

practice.q: What does this output? FOR i = 1 TO 3: OUTPUT i * 2
Write an IF... THEN... ELSE for a prayer reminder: if time is 13:00 or later and Dhuhr not prayed, remind.
practice.a: IF time >= 13:00 AND prayed = false THEN OUTPUT 'Pray Dhuhr' ELSE OUTPUT 'Well done'.

independent.q: Core: Write an algorithm for a 'guess the number' game that uses sequence, selection and iteration. Label each.
independent.a: Set secret; REPEAT input guess; IF guess = secret THEN 'Correct' ELSE IF guess < secret 'Higher' ELSE 'Lower'; UNTIL guess = secret.
independent.model: Teacher writes the first two lines: 'secret = 7' (sequence) and 'REPEAT' (iteration), naming each.

independent.q: Extend: Trace: total = 0; FOR i = 2 TO 8 STEP 2: total = total + i. Output?
Stretch: Explain the difference between a FOR loop and a WHILE loop, with an example of each.
independent.a: FOR repeats a set number of times (count to 10); WHILE repeats until a condition changes (while not boiled).

exit.q: IF... THEN... ELSE is... A) sequence B) selection C) iteration
Big question: name the three building blocks of every algorithm.

lessons.homework: Find one example of sequence, selection and iteration in your daily routine and write each as a line of pseudocode.
lessons.send: SEND: colour-coded labels (sequence blue, selection orange, iteration green). EAL: sentence frames 'This is selection because...'. Stretch: nested selection inside a loop.

The water cycle: a process that repeats

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Think like a computer: algorithms
lessons.title: Flowcharts and pseudocode
lessons.bigQuestion: Why would a programmer draw a diagram before writing any code?
objectives: To understand how flowcharts and pseudocode represent the same algorithm
successCriteria: All: name the flowchart symbols (terminal, process, decision, input/output)
Most: draw a flowchart with a decision
Some: convert a flowchart into pseudocode and back
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: following a key (yes/no questions) to identify plants or animals
lessons.smsc: Social: planning clearly so others can understand and check our work

keywords.def: a diagram that shows an algorithm with symbols and arrows
an algorithm written in structured English, like code
a diamond symbol with a yes/no question
the start or stop symbol (rounded box)

hook.text: Why would a programmer draw a diagram before writing any code?
hook.a: To see the whole plan, spot mistakes early and share it with others who do not read code.

starter.q: 'Repeat until full' is...
Output of FOR i = 1 TO 4: OUTPUT i * i?
What are the two kinds of loop?
What is a condition?
starter.a: A statement that is true or false.

teach.heading: Flowchart symbols
teach.note: Draw each symbol live in diagrams.net.

teach.heading: A flowchart with a decision
bullets: A decision has two exits: Yes and No
teach.note: Model the 'Can I use this app?' flowchart (age 13 rule).

model.problem: Flowchart: can a pupil create an account on an app with a minimum age of 13?
steps: Yes: output 'You may ask a parent to set it up'
model.answer: Start, input, decision with two outputs, stop

teach.heading: The same in pseudocode
bullets: A loop back becomes WHILE or REPEAT
teach.note: Compare side by side.

code.text:
INPUT age
IF age >= 13 THEN
    OUTPUT "You may ask a parent to set it up"
ELSE
    OUTPUT "Not yet"
ENDIF

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: Which flowchart symbol holds a yes/no question?
check.why: Diamonds are decisions; rectangles are processes; parallelograms are input and output; rounded rectangles are start and stop.

practice.q: Draw a flowchart: input a number, output 'even' or 'odd'.
practice.a: Start; input n; decision: n MOD 2 = 0?; yes: output 'even'; no: output 'odd'; stop.
practice.model: Teacher draws it in diagrams.net, saying the symbol name before each shape.

practice.q: Write the even/odd flowchart as pseudocode.
practice.a: INPUT n; IF n MOD 2 = 0 THEN OUTPUT 'even' ELSE OUTPUT 'odd' ENDIF

independent.q: Core: Draw a flowchart in diagrams.net (or on paper) for a password check: allow 3 tries, then lock. Paste a picture into the portal.
independent.a: Start; tries = 0; loop: input password; decision correct? yes: 'Welcome', stop; no: tries + 1; decision tries = 3? yes: 'Locked', stop; no: back to input.
independent.model: Teacher draws the first three symbols: Start, 'tries = 0', 'INPUT password'.

independent.q: Extend: Write your flowchart as pseudocode.
independent.a: tries = 0; REPEAT INPUT p; tries = tries + 1 UNTIL p = correct OR tries = 3; IF p = correct THEN 'Welcome' ELSE 'Locked'.

independent.q: Stretch: Explain one advantage of a flowchart and one of pseudocode.
independent.a: Flowchart: shows the flow visually for anyone; pseudocode: closer to code, quicker to turn into a program.

exit.q: Start and stop use the... A) diamond B) rounded rectangle C) parallelogram
Big question: give one reason to draw a flowchart before coding.
exit.a: To plan and check the logic and spot mistakes before writing code.

lessons.homework: Draw a flowchart for deciding whether to take an umbrella (check the forecast; if rain is likely, take it).
lessons.send: SEND: symbol cards to drag into place. EAL: symbol names with shapes. Stretch: flowchart with a loop and a counter.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Think like a computer: algorithms
lessons.title: Testing and debugging algorithms; unit quiz
lessons.bigQuestion: An exam grader gives a 'pass' for 50 and above. Which single score would you test first, and why?
objectives: To understand how testing with normal, boundary and invalid data finds errors in an algorithm
successCriteria: All: find an error in an algorithm by tracing it
Most: choose normal, boundary and invalid test data
Some: fix a logic error and prove the fix with a test
lessons.smsc: Moral: honesty in checking our own work carefully (amanah in what we produce)

keywords.def: values chosen to check an algorithm works
a value at the edge of what is allowed
a mistake that gives the wrong result without crashing
find and fix errors

hook.text: An exam grader gives a 'pass' for 50 and above. Which single score would you test first, and why?
hook.a: 50: the boundary. It is where mistakes like > instead of >= hide.

starter.q: Which symbol is a decision?
Name the three building blocks of algorithms.
What is abstraction?
starter.a: Removing detail that does not matter.

starter.q: Output of FOR i = 1 TO 3: total = total + i (total starts 0)?

teach.heading: Why test?
bullets: Algorithms can look right and be wrong
teach.note: A logic error does not crash: it quietly gives the wrong answer.

teach.heading: Three kinds of test data
bullets: Invalid: values that should be rejected
teach.note: Pass mark 50, scores 0 to 100.

teach.heading: Find the bug
teach.note: Model.

model.problem: IF score > 50 THEN OUTPUT 'Pass' ELSE OUTPUT 'Fail'. Test with 50.
steps: Actual: Fail, so there is a logic error
Fix: IF score >= 50; re-test 50 gives Pass

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: Ages 11 to 16 are allowed. Which is boundary test data?
check.why: 16 is at the edge of the allowed range; 13 is normal; 25 and 'eleven' are invalid.

practice.q: Give normal, boundary and invalid data for 'enter a month number 1 to 12'.
practice.model: Teacher writes the range on a number line and marks the edges 1 and 12, then picks a middle value and a nonsense value.

practice.q: Find the bug: 'FOR i = 1 TO 10: OUTPUT i' should output 1 to 9.
practice.a: The loop runs to 10; change to FOR i = 1 TO 9.

independent.q: Core: Write a test plan (4 tests) for the password-lock flowchart from last lesson.
independent.a: Correct first time; wrong then right; 3 wrong (locked); empty password.
independent.model: Teacher writes test 1: 'Input correct password first time; expected: Welcome'.
